analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 25, Federal Land Bank of Wichita, Petitioner v. Board of County Commissioners of the County of Keowa, State of Kansas, in Alabama. Mr. Doolittle. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case is here on a writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of the State of Kansas. It presents a relatively narrow issue, but one of considerable importance in the administration of the federal farm credit system. That is, whether a certain personal property owned by a federal land bank consisting of a royalty interest in an oil and gas lease is subject to taxation by a state in view of Section 26 of the Federal Farm Loan Act, which exempts federal land banks from all taxation by federal, state, local, and municipal authorities except for taxation upon real estate. The Kansas courts have held that this property may be taxed, and your petitioner, the Federal Land Bank of Wichita, earnestly submits that this was error and that the judgment below should be reversed. Now, before I reach the facts of this case, I should like to very briefly invite the Court's recollection to the character of the federal farm credit system and particularly of federal land banks. Under the terms of the Federal Farm Loan Act of 1916 and subsequent legislation, the United States is divided into 12 farm credit districts. In each of these, there is a federal land bank, which is one of several types of specialized rural credit institutions, all of which are under the direct supervision of the Farm Credit Administration in Washington. These federal land banks were created by Congress in 1960 for one central purpose, and that is to provide farmers with long-term loans for agricultural purposes in exchange for mortgages on agricultural land at the lowest possible interest rates. The whole structure and functioning of these land banks is directed toward that one central purpose. Now, the United States government furnished practically all of the capital to get these federal land banks started in 1917, and then later on in the Depression years, they had to contribute a good bit more capital to keep the banks going. However, all of this money has been paid back to the federal government, and at the present time there is no government money in the federal land banks. All of the stock in the federal land banks is owned by federal land bank associations, which are local cooperative associations owned entirely by borrowers from the farm credit system. Now, for example, there are 77 of these local associations in the 9th Farm Credit District, which is the four-state area that your petitioner serves. A farmer who wishes to borrow from the farm credit system, in other words, who wants a long-term loan for agricultural purposes in exchange for a first mortgage on his farm, joins one of these associations by subscribing to its stock in the amount of 5% of the loan. In turn, the association, in order to obtain funds from the federal land bank for the loan, subscribes to 5% of the stock of the federal land bank. Now, in each instance, this stock is retired as soon as the loan to which it relates is repaid, so that at all times the only individuals that have any proprietary interest in the federal land banks are the individual farmer borrowers. Now, the federal land banks obtain the bulk of the money that they lend through the issuance of federal farm loan bonds, either individually or, much more frequently, in consolidation with all of the other federal land banks. After they pay the interest on these bonds, or retire any of them that may have matured, pay their operating expenses, and then make the required additions to their reserves, the federal land banks are authorized to declare dividends on their stock out of any profits that they may have had with the approval of the Farm Credit Administration. These are paid, of course, to the federal land bank associations who own the stock in the banks themselves, and in turn these associations are authorized to declare dividends on their stock. Of course, these dividends then go to the individual farmer borrowers and have the effect, which is specifically contemplated by the framers of this legislation, of reducing the rate of interest that they actually have to pay on their loans. Now, the facts in this case are not at all in dispute. In 1941, one of the loans for which the petitioner had taken a first mortgage on farmland was in default, and the bank instituted foreclosure proceedings. It acquired the farm in question at a sheriff's sale, and shortly thereafter sold it to its present owner. Now, as a result of that sale, the petitioner received a price sufficient to cover its loss on the default and its expenses in connection with the foreclosure. But in conveying the property, the bank reserved an undivided one-half interest in the minerals underlying the land. This reservation was for 20 years, and for so long thereafter as minerals were being developed on the premises. That's right, sir. In 1955, a pool of gas was discovered in this area, and in that same year, the Federal Land Bank granted a 10-year oil and gas lease of their interest in this property to an oil company. In 1957, the Respondent Board of County Commissioners of Kiowa County, Kansas, levied a personal property tax on the petitioner's royalty interest in this oil and gas lease. Now, I want particularly to note that the petitioner does regularly pay real property taxes on this mineral interest, and compilible mineral interest, as would be indicated by its exemption, which accepts real property interests. The tax involved in this case is solely on the royalty interest, which under the law of Kansas is personal property. The Federal Land Bank brought suit... That is conceded. That is conceded. The Federal Land Bank brought suit against the appropriate county officials in the District Court of Kiowa County for an injunction against the levy and assessment of this tax. On the ground, Section 26 of the Federal Farm Loan Act expressly exempts them from such taxation. The trial court denied the injunction, and the Supreme Court of Kansas affirmed it. Your petitioner is here today respectfully urging that the judgment below must be reversed if the congressional purpose in enacting the Federal Farm Loan Act is properly to be served. Now, it was only natural that Congress, in establishing instrumentalities through which farmers were to be able to obtain long-term loans at the lowest possible interest rates, should exempt these instrumentalities from taxation. And in point of fact, it did so in the most unmistakable and unqualified terms. Section 26 of the Federal Farm Loan Act, which is set forth in an appendix to our brief, provides that every Federal Land Bank and every Federal Land Bank association, including the capital and reserve or surplus therein and the income derived therefrom, shall be exempt from Federal, State, Municipal, and Local taxation, except taxes upon real estate. As we have discussed at pages 18 and 19 of our brief, the legislative history makes it apparent that Congress regarded this tax exemption as essential to the accomplishment of its purposes in enacting this legislation and saw this as the only way of assuring that farmers could be gotten cheaper money than would be available to them through ordinary commercial channels. Now, in the Bismarck Lumber case, that's the Federal Land Bank against Bismarck Lumber Company, which is cited and discussed at page 9 of our brief. This court confirmed this view of the congressional purpose when it said of the tax exemption section, broad construction is indicated by Congress's intention to advance credit to farm borrowers at the lowest possible interest rate. Your Honors, I submit that not even a broad construction is necessary to bring property involved in this case but within the terms of the statutory exemption. Property is concededly, not within the real property, exception to the exemption. It is concededly owned by the bank. This is not the sort of case where, for example, the burden of the tax might fall upon purchasers from the bank, vendors to the bank, employees of the bank, contractors with the bank. There's no question, no doubt at all, but that the bank itself, which is concededly a Federal instrumentality, will have to pay this tax directly out of its own resources. And by so doing, it must pro tanto render itself less able to carry out the congressional function that it has, and that is to provide farmers with mortgage money at the lowest possible price. I suggest that the square applicability of the Section 26 tax exemption could not be more apparent. But the court below sought to avoid this conclusion by holding that to the Federal Land Bank was not engaged in a governmental function when it retained the mineral interest upon which this tax is based. And this, because the bank had fully recouped its loss in the loan on default and had covered its expenses in the foreclosure when it took this particular interest. And from this, the court concludes that the bank was therefore not entitled to the tax exemption granted by Congress. I submit that this argument falls on several grounds. In the first place, this court has repeatedly rejected any notion that a distinction between governmental and non-governmental functions is applicable to the activities of the federal government or its instrumentalities. The federal government being one of delegated powers, all of its lawful activities are governmental, whether they are performed directly or through a corporation. That doctrine was applied to the federal land banks in the Bismarck Lumber case, which I've already cited to you. There, a state sought to apply a sales tax to lumber and other building materials that the federal land bank purchased for necessary repairs and improvements to buildings on property that it had acquired through foreclosure. This court, in holding that the Section 26 exemption was applicable, did not concern itself with whether or not the bank had to make these improvements in the buildings on the property in order to get its money back out of the loan. Since it was plainly a proper function, indeed, I submit a duty of the bank to get as much out of the sale of this foreclosed property as possible. This court had no difficulty at all in finding the statutory tax exemption applicable. Secondly, I submit that it's plain that the federal land bank's retention of mineral interests, such as those involved in this case, contribute directly and importantly to their accomplishment of the aims for which Congress established them in 1916. As we pointed out at pages 17 and 18 of our brief, Congress intended not only that the federal land bank system be self-sustaining, but that it be profitable in order that dividends could be passed on down to the farmer borrowers as effective reductions in their interest rates. In view of that intention, it is not difficult to perceive why it is appropriate, indeed necessary, that the federal land banks have access to auxiliary sources of income, such as the income from these mineral reservations. Now, in some instances, for example, the income from these mineral reservations may wholly or partly offset a loss that the bank might sustain on the particular loan in question, and the court below clearly recognizes that in its opinion, in that event, this would be a proper governmental function on the part of the land bank, or the income from the retention of one of these mineral interests may make up for losses on other pieces of property as to which no such compensating offset was available, and as to that type of thing, the court below seems to indicate that it would regard that as a proper governmental function on the part of the land bank, or such income from mineral reservations might contribute to the reserves of the bank in order to provide an offset to possible future losses as a result of defaults in loans. The court did not specifically touch on that, nor was it asked to do so, but that is a type of purpose whose value was strikingly illustrated during the depression years, when the federal land banks had to look to the United States government for contributions to its capital in order to maintain their solvency. Indeed, the Senate hearings that we have cited at pages 24 and 25 of our brief describe an example of a federal land bank that was brought to self-sustaining sufficiency only with the aid of income from such mineral reservations as we're talking about here. Finally, and no less legitimately, I submit, that the mineral reservation income is not needed for any of the purposes that I've indicated already. it would be available for the distribution of dividends to the farmer borrowers, thus fulfilling the congressional purpose of bringing them mortgage money at the lowest possible interest rates. Mr. Doolittle, I'm a little bit lost to understand how any of these questions develop because isn't it true under the law of Kansas personal property taxes were assessed against the person? That is correct. Now then, how could Kansas, Iowa County, Kansas, assess this tax against this bank and at the same time deny it owned the property? Well, Mr. Justice Whitaker, the bank does not in fact deny that, I'm sorry, the state does not deny that the bank owns the property. Then how, how is it relevant to say that it ought not to own it? That's what they must say if they say that they have no proper business purpose in owning it. Aren't they stopped to say that when they've actually assessed the tax against the state? I believe it would be a reasonable argument that they should be, Mr. Justice Whitaker. But in point of fact, that is the essence of their argument that because, in their opinion, the bank should not own this property under these circumstances, they say there are some circumstances when it would be proper. But since they say that the bank should not own the property under these circumstances, then it is not entitled to the tax exemption. What's the source of the should not? Well, it is their contention, the contention of the state of Kansas, arguing here, although I don't believe that the court below so held that the federal land banks are not authorized to hold this kind of property. Now, the court below went no further than to say that since this is not a proper governmental function, that it is simply not entitled to a tax exemption. I understand it. Do I understand that they are not a proper governmental function, that they go on to distinction to the court which used to make in the past more than nowadays, differentiating between so-called proprietary functions and governmental? Indeed so. Or do they suggest this is ultra-viry and therefore they can't come in under the umbrella of the federal bank act? Well, as I read the opinion of the court below, they are relying almost exclusively on the proprietary governmental distinction. Now, I think that the state, as it argues to this court, is going more to the ultra-virus point. And I would like to deal with that. Before you see that, is there a suggestion that although either by explicit authorization or by interpretation of the scope of the function of these banks, practically they may have been allowed to exercise and therefore presumably the authorization is to be inferred, that Canada or any state can construe what the statute allows and disallows? Well, certainly the effect of the decision below is at least if interpreted as the state of Kansas would have it interpreted, the state is being permitted to determine what kinds of property and what kinds of activities this federal agency should engage in. without any reference to what has as a matter of business practice been the allowable area of activity of these banks. That's right, Mr. Justice. To the stated taxes expressing this tax a person against the federal land tax. Yes, that's right, expressly. Now, then, how, what, all the questions are you interested? I submit, Mr. Justice Whitaker, that there really is no other question. I'd like to assess this tax as personal property without an individual or corporation without a union that you don't do this. That's what makes you much like to assess it. That's right, Mr. Justice. But their contention is, and as I say, particularly as expressed in this court, is that it was beyond the authority of the bank to hold this kind of property and that the exemption doesn't apply to any property held without authority. Well, if you start with the tenant court's premise, you begin where they begin, namely, that there is in law a cleavage between, in the activities of governmental order, that there is a cleavage between so-called governmental functions and so-called proprietary functions, then it doesn't require greater studentness nor is it privileged to argue that the exemption statute is being a student at large. Isn't that what they're doing? That exactly is it, Mr. Rahn. Now, although, as I say, the court below does not seem to have gone so far, the respondents do argue that even if these mineral reservations do contribute directly and importantly to the achievement of the governmental purposes for which the Federal Land Bank was created. Still, they are unlawful and not entitled to tax exemption because, as they assert, Federal Land Banks are not expressly and by statute authorized to invest in mineral reservations. Now, at the outset, I should like to emphasize one point, and that is, as the respondents recognize in their brief, what we are talking about here is investments on the part of the Federal Land Bank and nothing more. This case does not involve Federal Land Banks going into different businesses, such as the business of mineral exploration, production, or marketing. And so, when the respondents argue that to reverse the decision below will enable Federal Land Banks to operate tax-free filling stations and the like, they are raising a specter that is simply not for this court. Similar procession of absurdities was marshaled in the Bismarck Lumber case, where it was contended that to sustain the exemption there would enable Federal Land Banks to go into the business of operating farms, lumber mills, even manufacturing plans tax-free. The argument is no more convincing today than it was then when the court rejected it. It's too little. If you put me up and let it collected all the things in which this court has tried to put an end to this assumption that the government of the United States will private things that are new or here before not having been done by the government. There are a great many of them and I would not care to claim that we have assembled all of them. More particularly because in this one case that I've cited to you several times today, the court so clearly stated this with respect to the Federal Land Banks that it seems scarcely necessary to go any further. Now of course the statutory scheme contemplates that the great bulk of the Federal Land Bank's funds shall be invested in first mortgage loans. After all, that's why the banks were established in the first place. I don't suppose that it would be sound investment policy for them to devote all of their funds in that way. And Congress plainly intended that the banks should have considerable scope in the investment of their reserves and surplus, subject always, I emphasize this, subject always to the direct supervision of the Farm Credit Administration. For example, Section 23 of the Act confers general authority on the Federal Land Banks to invest their reserves in accordance with rules and regulations of the Farm Credit Administration. Section 5 specifies that a quick asset portion of the capital of the Federal Land Banks is to be invested, again, in accordance with rules and regulations of the Farm Credit Administration. Now, there's no specific provision concerning the investment of the bank's surpluses, but I submit that the power of the banks to invest their surplus is fairly inferable from the character and statutory context, again, however, only under the direct and continuing supervision of the Farm Credit Administration. And if the statute doesn't make clear that the banks have reasonable freedom to invest their resources, the legislative history certainly does. The attitude of the framers of this legislation on this point is typified by a statement of Congressman Phelan of Massachusetts, who was one of the managers of this bill in the House, he made this statement in opposition to an amendment that he thought would limit the investment powers of the bank. I'm quoting from 53 Congressional Records, 79-98, which I regret does not appear in our brief. The whole theory of the cooperative plan is that the funds of the bank shall be used to the best advantage so that the farmer will be getting a profit out of the system and not be absolutely obliged to suffer in lack of profits to the bank because the bank is handicapped and tied hand and foot by explicit provisions of the law from investing its money. Could you give that citation again? Yes, Mr. Justice Harlan, that's 53 Congressional Record, 79-98. Now, I submit that the investment authority of the federal land banks is broad enough to comprehend the investments in mineral interests that are involved in this case, subject always to the approval of the Farm Credit Administration. And in point of fact, the Farm Credit Administration has, by regulation, specifically approved of the banks retaining these interests. And the regulation in question is cited in the appendix to our brief, is set forth, I should say. Now, as an alternative argument, the respondents contend that the federal land bank's retention of this property violates the specific prohibition in Section 13 IV of the Act against holding title and possession of foreclosed real estate for more than five years without the special approval of the Farm Credit Administration. The court below did not seem to adopt this position wholeheartedly, and for the reasons that we've stated, pages 21 to 24 of our brief, we don't believe that there's any substance to them. But even if the respondent is correct, that there is some colorable question as to the authority of the federal land banks to retain the mineral interests, either because of a lack of affirmative authorization or because of some negative prohibition we submit that there is no basis for the state court stripping the bank of its statutory exemption in this instance. The supervision of the federal land banks has been specifically entrusted by Congress to the Farm Credit Administration, the United States Agency, and not to the courts. That agency's construction of the federal land bank's powers under this complex and comprehensive statute should be given great weight and should not be subject to collateral attack, not at least in the absence of fraud or some comparably grave defect. When an agency has exercised supervisory responsibility honestly and in the manner that it believes best calculated to carry out the purposes of the legislation, we submit that the proper recourse for the correction of any alleged errors is to Congress. Certainly it is not to the state courts. I should like to reserve the rest of my time for the debate. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. Before commencing with the argument, I would like to clarify the position that we take on the question of the distinction between governmental and proprietary function. We do not feel that that distinction has any relevance or materiality in this case. The line of cleavage which we wish to draw here is between the authorized governmental functions of the bank and the functions or holding the property which they may in fact engage in, but which transgresses or goes beyond the bounds of their statutory authority. the court below discussed... Now, do you mind to clarify that a little more? You mean these are activities which are, you call them ultra-violence? Is that a fair? That's a fair term. Yes, Your Honor. Yes, Your Honor. So if they go outside of those, they require those forbidden activities. You said they may engage in them. Wouldn't they be forbidden? If Congress establishes an agency, it says your powers are, one, two, three, four, they can't do six, seven, eight, can't they? That's precisely our argument, Your Honor. And when they do, in fact, I mean, it's human to err, when they do, in fact, do six, seven, and eight, then it calls into question whether or not the governmental tax immunity, which is based on the need to protect governmental functions, can be said to apply to them in so transgressing the bounds of their authority. For present purposes, at all events, you're not concerned with what any proprietary consequences may follow. No. Six, seven, eight, the order says they have immunity, only four, one, two, three, four. Yes, Your Honor, and we're fully aware in Kansas of the fact that this court has long ago rejected the distinction between governmental and proprietary, and I would say in defense of the Kansas Supreme Court, I think counsel is misconstruing the opinion below. The Kansas court relied heavily on a Kansas case, and in that Kansas case, at that time the distinction between governmental and proprietary functions was in vogue. I think that counsel misconstrues the intent of the court below in their opinion. They did not mean to say that this was a proprietary function, since that distinction is no longer valid. They were quoting from this other case for the purpose of the reasoning that it contained regarding the scope of the tax exemption, and this was just an incidental aspect of it. I think counsel has misconstrued it and felt that they were, that they misunderstood this distinction. I don't believe the court did. I think they were clearly placing it on the distinction between the governmental functions that are authorized, one, two, three, and things they might in fact do, but which transgress their bounds. Well, then your position is that whatever the land bank does is, and so far as the term carries an irrelevant, a governmental function. But what the extent of the governmental function is is what you question. Yes, and we feel this is really a matter of statutory construction considering the Federal Farm Loan Act. Now, our point of difference, then, is how far they can go in the ownership of real property and the incidents of it. And it is our position on that that the... Mr. Waddle, is a real property tax involved here? Well, Your Honor, let me explain how this aspect of it comes into being. The mineral estate which the bank retained in 1946 when they conveyed away the surface estate and the other half of the mineral estate is under Kansas property law, real estate. Sir, I'm familiar with that, but we haven't that before us. Only in that it is a necessary part and parcel of considering whether this leasing of the real property is beyond their power. We're saying that the holding of the mineral estate was beyond their power and therefore leasing it to a oil producer or production purposes being simply an incident of the ownership was likewise unlawful. so that the unlawful holding of the, the unlawful leasing of the mineral estate for production is part and parcel of the unlawful ownership of the real property mineral estate. May I ask you this? You can't separate them, in other words. Does not a taxing authority, the county, the Kansas, by assessing a personal property tax against you admit you own the property? Yes, Your Honor, most certainly, and we certainly affirm that they have the de facto title to this property. Well, we're not here asking this court for the relief that they order the land bank to divest themselves of this property. The only reason that we question their right under the federal statute to own this property is to determine its status as it pertains to its taxability or immunity from tax under the concept of governmental tax immunity. It's possible, and there are many cases dealing with corporations, for a corporation to in fact have the de facto title to property, even though under its charter it does not have the power to do so. So we are affirming that the bank owns this property. They are the owner. No one else owns it. It owns this mineral estate, and they are the owner of the lease that they've given on it, and therefore they are the proper party subject to the tax. But we are saying in retaining this mineral estate in 1946, after they had fully recouped their mortgage debt on the property, that they exceeded the power granted them under the Federal Farm Loan Act to hold real estate. And when they stepped beyond the bounds of the functions and the powers granted them by Congress, they likewise stepped beyond the bounds of governmental tax immunity. In fact, you say, because they buy property, if they have property, but it's unlawful for them to have and own. If they lose that tax community on that property, then they own and own them in violation of taxes. Yes, Mr. Justice Black, and I believe this court in Bank of Commerce v. Tennessee long ago had occasion to consider a similar situation arising under a state law exempting the property of a state bank where the exemption, as here, was in its terms absolute, and it exempted all real property of the state bank. However, in another provision of the state law of Tennessee, there was a restriction. As we say, there is a restriction here on the power of the state bank to hold real property. The state bank did, in fact, acquire a piece of property. In that case, it was the building in which they operated their bank. They leased part of that building to another person for revenue purposes. the state court and this court affirming wholeheartedly said that in leasing that real estate, even though the use of it for the bank was proper, that in leasing it to others for revenue purposes, they stepped beyond the bounds of their authority. That usage of it, that ownership for that purpose, was unlawful. And encompassed within that finding was the fact that the bank did, in fact, own it. And they said, therefore, the granting of the tax immunity was never intended to cover property which the bank might, in fact, acquire, but acquire unlawfully in excess of its delegated powers. I would think that if the bank couldn't own the property, then someone else owns it, and Kansas couldn't, therefore, assess it to the bank, would have to assess it against the owners, or assess it against the bank as a trustee. Well, Your Honor, that would require saying, and we feel that the bank does own this property. And there are many cases in which corporations, for example, have purchased property which the charter did not permit them to purchase. And, in fact, in the Bank of Tennessee, that was inherent. They were owning this property in part for a purpose they were not entitled to do. Nevertheless, they are the owner, de facto, if you please, but not de jure, of this property. And the state, in looking about at the property within its jurisdiction, when it comes across this piece of property, it must determine, is this property taxable? The fact that the Federal Land Bank has its title on the property and is the de facto owner, we do not think precludes an inquiry into the question of whether they're holding that property within the scope of their lawfully delegated federal authority from Congress. We do not think they are. And, therefore, we do not feel that the status of this property, even though it's owned by them, is entitled to be clothed with governmental tax immunity. This court has stated many times that the justification and the reason for governmental tax immunity is to protect the functions and property of government. That when a federal agency or instrumentality is engaged in furtherance of its lawfully delegated federal functions, it must needs be protected by governmental tax immunity. We have no question with that, doctor. We think that inherent in that statement, there's a corollary rule that where an agency, in fact, exceeds that power and is holding property as the bank is here in a collateral sideline business activity, after its power to hold it has ceased and terminated, that the reason for the rule of tax immunity fails of application, and, therefore, the rule itself must fail. And that is precisely what this court said in a similar case, construing a state statute in the state banks' power. He said it was never the intention to immunize any more property that a bank could lawfully hold when the state, in that case, the state legislature gave a tax immunity to real property. We're saying here that when Congress, in Section 26 of the Farm Loan Act of 1916, immunized all personal property, that there was property, was an inherent limitation or qualification or intention on their part, that they were talking about only that personal property which the bank might lawfully acquire, own, and use in furtherance of the federal functions they were delegating to the bank in other sections of the Act. We're saying here that upon an examination of the other sections of the Act, and particularly the consideration of the overall function of the bank, and particularly Section 5, which spells out the limit of its authority of the whole real property, that the ownership in this particular case, under these particular facts and circumstances, is not authorized in some other section of the Act, and therefore Section 26, which immunizes personal property, being no broader than the Act itself and the powers delegated by the Act, does not extend to cover this ownership, this usage of the property. The Farm Credit Administration is purported at least to approve this acquisition. Yes, Your Honor, and our position on that is that the limitation on the power to hold real property cannot be expanded under this clause relating to the special approval of the Farm Credit Administration. In fact, we think that section was inserted by Congress to serve as a check on the individual banks out in the field to make sure that they were holding real property, where they did hold real property at the point of five years, there would be cause to be made a review to determine if they were still holding it within the scope of their authority, and that the special approval was not intended as a backdoor means of blossoming their authority out to hold real property for any purpose so long as it is profitable. Now, it is a fundamental rule applicable to all state, federal, state, and local instrumentalities and agencies that they possess only those powers which are granted them by the statute, and that any power not expressly granted them by statute is impliedly denied to them. Now, in this case, we feel that that rule applies. They also feel that there is a section of the Act which is of application here, section 14, which in its terms states that the bank is expressly denied the power of engaging in any banking business or any other business activity not expressly authorized by some other section of the Act. Now, nowhere in the Act is there a statement of the bank's power to hold real property for speculation and profit as the bank has done in this case.
